chapters.n: Jacob, Nephi’s younger brother born in the wilderness, now takes up the record. About 55 years after Lehi left Jerusalem (roughly 545 BC), Nephi gave him charge of the small plates.

f.g: Lehi left around 600 BC, so this is about 545 BC.

chapters.n: Nephi told Jacob to record only the most precious things and to touch history only lightly. These plates were for sacred, spiritual matters.
Detailed history went on Nephi’s “other plates” (the large plates). Jacob was to keep the small plates and pass them down through his family.
Sacred sermons, great revelations, and prophecies were to be recorded in summary—“the heads of them”—for Christ’s sake and the people’s.

f.g: Main points, headings, summaries.

chapters.n: Because of their faith and deep concern, the Lord revealed to them what would happen to their people in the future.

f.g: Deep concern and care, not nervous worry.

chapters.n: Through many revelations and prophecy, they knew about Christ and his coming kingdom centuries before his birth.
They worked hard to bring people to Christ so they could enter God’s rest—unlike ancient Israel, who rebelled in the wilderness and were barred from the promised land.

f.g: Israel’s rebellions in the wilderness that provoked God (Numbers 14).

chapters.n: Jacob longs for all to believe in Christ, “view his death,” and bear the world’s scorn for following him. So he accepts Nephi’s commission.
As Nephi grew old, he anointed a new king to rule after him.

f.g: Consecrated with oil, the ancient Israelite rite for installing a king.

chapters.n: The people loved Nephi deeply. He had protected them, even wielding Laban’s sword, and worked all his life for their good.
To honor him, the people called each later king “second Nephi,” “third Nephi,” and so on, whatever the king’s actual name.

f.g: A royal title, much like “Pharaoh” or “Caesar.”

chapters.n: The great prophet and founder Nephi died—a simple, quiet line marking the end of an era.

f.g: Roughly 545 BC or a little after.

chapters.n: The people were divided into clans named after Lehi’s sons and companions.

f.g: Descendants of Zoram, Laban’s servant who joined Lehi’s family (1 Nephi 4:35).

chapters.n: Jacob simplifies: those who seek to destroy Nephi’s people he will call Lamanites; those friendly to Nephi, Nephites. The labels describe loyalty more than bloodline.

f.w: Lamanites that seek to destroy the people of Nephi

chapters.n: Under the second king, the people began to harden and indulge in sins like David and Solomon’s many wives and concubines.

f.g: Secondary wives with lower legal status.

chapters.n: They also chased after gold and silver and became proud.
So Jacob preached to them at the temple, after first receiving his “errand,” or assignment, from the Lord.

f.g: A commissioned message or assignment.

chapters.n: Nephi had consecrated Jacob and his brother Joseph as priests and teachers.
They took their calling seriously, believing that if they failed to teach diligently, the people’s sins would be on their heads. Faithful teaching keeps one’s “garments” clean.

f.g: Do the calling fully and honorably.

f.w: their blood might not come upon our garments

chapters.n: A heading introduces Jacob’s temple sermon to the Nephites after Nephi’s death.
Jacob comes to the temple to fulfill his duty and to “rid his garments” of the people’s sins by warning them.

f.w: rid my garments of your sins

f.g: Seriousness and gravity.

chapters.n: He has always been diligent, but today he feels much heavier concern for their souls.
So far, he acknowledges, they have obeyed the Lord’s word.
With God’s help he can discern their thoughts: they are beginning to sin in ways that horrify both him and God.
It pains Jacob, even shames him before God, to have to expose their hearts’ wickedness.
Worse, wives and children are present—tender, pure-hearted people whom his words may hurt.

f.g: Sensitive, pure, easily wounded.

chapters.n: They came hoping for healing words from God, not condemnation.
Jacob is burdened that, instead of healing those already wounded by their husbands’ sins, his strict message may deepen their pain.

f.w: daggers placed to pierce their souls
f.g: A vivid image of words that cut deeply.

chapters.n: Still, he must obey God and speak openly before the innocent and the brokenhearted, under God’s all-seeing gaze.
He will speak plainly, because the Lord told him the day before to go to the temple and deliver this message.

f.w: get thou up into the temple

chapters.n: First problem: many are hunting for gold, silver, and precious ores in this abundant promised land.
God blessed them with riches, but those with more became proud, flaunted expensive clothes, and looked down on and mistreated poorer brothers.

f.g: Stubbornness and arrogance.

chapters.n: Does God approve? No—he condemns it, and judgment will come quickly if they persist.
Jacob wishes God would show them how easily his glance could humble them to the dust.

f.g: Humble you completely.

chapters.n: He pleads that God would free them from this sin and that they would listen, not letting pride destroy their souls.
The cure for pride: think of others as equals, be friendly to all, and share generously so they can prosper too.

f.g: Generous with your possessions.

f.w: Think of your brethren like unto yourselves

chapters.n: Priorities: seek God’s kingdom before riches.

f.w: seek ye for the kingdom of God

chapters.n: After gaining a hope in Christ, you may seek riches—but for doing good: clothing the naked, feeding the hungry, freeing captives, and caring for the sick.
Jacob challenges those who used God’s gifts as an excuse to oppress their neighbors: what do they have to say?
Every person is equally precious to God. All come from dust and were created for the same purpose—to keep his commandments and glorify him.

f.w: the one being is as precious in his sight as the other
all flesh is of the dust

chapters.n: Jacob finishes on pride, but says a “grosser crime”—a more serious sin—still weighs on him.

f.g: A more serious, flagrant sin.

chapters.n: The Lord says the people misuse scripture, excusing sexual sin by pointing to David and Solomon’s many wives.

f.g: Sexual immorality.

chapters.n: The Lord declares that David and Solomon’s many wives and concubines were abominable to him—in their case, taken without his approval.
God led Lehi’s family out of Jerusalem to raise up a righteous branch from Joseph’s descendants.

f.g: Lehi descended from Joseph of Egypt through Manasseh.

chapters.n: So God will not allow this people to repeat the sins of ancient Israel.
The rule: each man may have only one wife, and no concubines.
God delights in women’s chastity and hates sexual sin. Purity, faithfulness, and the dignity of women matter deeply to him.

f.g: Sexual purity; faithfulness within marriage.

chapters.n: The people must keep God’s commandments, or the land itself will be cursed because of them.

An important exception: if God wants to “raise up seed,” he will command plural marriage; otherwise monogamy is the law. Latter-day Saints cite this verse to explain why plural marriage was practiced only when divinely commanded.
The Lord has seen the sorrow and heard the weeping of women in Jerusalem and everywhere, wounded by their husbands’ wickedness.
He will not allow the cries of Nephite women to rise against their men.
Men must not exploit women’s tenderness. If they do, God will send a severe curse, even to destruction.

f.g: Take advantage of, capture emotionally or socially.

chapters.n: Lehi had already taught these rules, so the people knew better and are under great condemnation.
Jacob says the Nephites have done worse than the Lamanites. They have broken their wives’ hearts and lost their children’s trust. Families suffer most from unfaithful fathers and husbands.

f.w: lost the confidence of your children
f.g: Lost their children’s trust and respect.

chapters.n: Jacob turns to the faithful, especially the wounded wives and children. If they look to God steadily and pray in faith, he will comfort them, defend them, and bring justice.

f.g: Steady, unwavering focus.

chapters.n: The pure in heart can lift up their heads and “feast upon his love” forever if they stay steady.
But woe to the impure. Unless they repent, the land is cursed for them, and the Lamanites—who are not guilty of these sins—will scourge them.

f.g: Punish severely, like a whip.

chapters.n: Soon, without repentance, Lamanites will take their lands and the Lord will lead the righteous away—which later happened under the first Mosiah.

f.w: lead away the righteous out from among you

chapters.n: Jacob shocks his audience: the Lamanites they despise are more righteous than they are, because Lamanites have kept the law of one wife and sexual purity.

f.w: cursing which hath come upon their skins

chapters.n: Because the Lamanites keep this commandment, God will be merciful and they will one day be a blessed people.
Lamanite families love one another. Their hostility comes from their fathers’ traditions. So how are the Nephites better in God’s eyes? Healthy family love counts heavily with God.
Jacob warns that at God’s judgment the Lamanites may look purer than the Nephites. He turns his listeners’ prejudice back on them: what matters to God is the heart, not appearance.

f.w: their skins will be whiter than yours
f.g: A rhetorical reversal: by God’s standard of purity, the Nephites would come off worse. The Church today teaches that skin color is never a sign of God’s favor or disfavor.

chapters.n: God commands them to stop insulting Lamanites for their skin or their sins. They should remember their own sins and that the Lamanites’ condition came from their ancestors’ choices.

f.g: Insult, speak abusively of.

chapters.n: Remember your children: your example has hurt them, and your sins could lead them to destruction—and you would answer for it.

f.w: their sins be heaped upon your heads

chapters.n: Wake up! Jacob urges them to rouse their souls from spiritual death, escape hell’s pains, and avoid the “second death”—final separation from God.

f.w: awake from the slumber of death

chapters.n: Jacob adds that he preached much more against sexual sin and every kind of wickedness, warning of their terrible consequences.

f.g: Lustful, indecent behavior.

chapters.n: Not even a hundredth of the people’s history fits here; their wars, conflicts, and kings are on the larger plates.
These are called the plates of Jacob, though Nephi made them. Jacob ends this sermon.

f.w: made by the hand of Nephi

chapters.n: Jacob has preached much, but engraving on metal plates is hard, so he writes little. What is written on plates will last.
Anything written on other materials will decay, but these few words on plates will tell future generations about their ancestors.

f.g: Perishable materials like parchment, wood, or bark rot over time.

chapters.n: Jacob hopes descendants will receive the record gratefully and learn about their ancestors with joy rather than sorrow or scorn.

f.g: Here meaning their founding ancestors—Lehi’s family.

chapters.n: The main purpose of the record: to show that these ancient people knew about Christ and hoped in him centuries before his birth, as all earlier prophets did.
They worshiped the Father in Christ’s name and kept the law of Moses because it pointed to him. Abraham offering Isaac foreshadowed the Father offering his Only Begotten Son.

f.g: Likeness, symbolic representation.

chapters.n: Studying the prophets, plus revelation and the spirit of prophecy, gave them unshaken faith—strong enough to command trees, mountains, or waves in Jesus’ name.
Yet God also shows them their weakness, so they know their power comes from his grace and kindness, not themselves.

f.g: God’s gracious willingness to stoop down to help humans.

chapters.n: God’s works and mysteries are beyond human discovery; we know his ways only by revelation. So never despise revelation.

f.w: despise not the revelations of God

chapters.n: God created the earth and humanity by his word. If he can do that, surely he can command the earth according to his will.

f.w: by the power of his word

chapters.n: Don’t try to advise God; take advice from him. He governs with wisdom, justice, and mercy.

f.w: seek not to counsel the Lord

chapters.n: Be reconciled to God through Christ’s Atonement. Through his power you can be resurrected and presented to God as Christ’s “firstfruits.”

f.g: The first, best part of a harvest offered to God—here the faithful presented to him.

chapters.n: Why not talk about the Atonement and seek to know Christ fully, just as people seek to understand the resurrection and the next life?
Prophecy should be plain and understandable. The Spirit tells the truth about things as they really are and will be; earlier prophets taught the same.
Many Jews rejected plainness and sought things beyond understanding. By “looking beyond the mark”—past the simple truth of Christ—they stumbled, and God allowed what they wanted.

f.g: Overlooking the target (Christ) in pursuit of complexity.

chapters.n: Led by the Spirit, Jacob prophesies that the Jews would reject the very stone—Christ—on which they could safely build.
Yet scripture says this stone will become the great, last, and only sure foundation for them.
How can a rejected stone become the “head of their corner”? Jacob raises the question he will answer next.
He promises to explain the mystery—if he can keep steady in the Spirit despite his intense concern for them. The answer is the allegory in chapter 5.

f.g: He answers with Zenos’s allegory of the olive tree.

chapters.n: Jacob answers the question from chapter 4 by quoting Zenos, a prophet of ancient Israel whose writings were on the brass plates but are not in our Bible.
Zenos addresses the whole house of Israel. What follows is the longest chapter in the Book of Mormon—an extended allegory.

f.g: Descendants of Jacob (Israel), and all who join God’s covenant.

chapters.n: Israel is like a tame, cultivated olive tree planted in God’s vineyard (the world). Over time it grows old and decays—a picture of spiritual decline and apostasy.

f.g: Grew old.

chapters.n: The master—the Lord—sees the decay and works to save the tree: pruning, digging, and nourishing it, hoping for new growth.

f.w: prune it, and dig about it
f.g: Real olive-growing techniques: cutting dead wood and loosening and fertilizing soil around roots.

chapters.n: The Lord does exactly what he said—sending prophets and correction to Israel.
After a long time a few young branches appear, but the top of the tree—Israel’s leaders and main body—begins to die.

f.g: The upper crown of the tree.

chapters.n: Grieved, the master has his servant bring branches from a wild olive tree (non-Israelites, the Gentiles) and plans to burn the withered main branches. Many relate this to Israel’s scattering and destruction.

f.g: Generally understood as the Gentiles—peoples outside the covenant.

chapters.n: The master takes young natural branches to graft wherever he chooses. Even if the root dies, he can preserve the fruit. This represents scattering Israelites around the world.

f.g: To insert a branch into another tree so it grows as part of it.

chapters.n: Wild branches are grafted into the original tree in place of those removed, and the dead branches are burned so they won’t clutter the vineyard.

f.g: Burden, clutter, take up space uselessly.

chapters.n: The servant obeys and grafts in the wild branches.
The master again nourishes the tree, hoping to preserve its roots—Israel’s covenant heritage and promises.

f.g: Roots likely represent the covenants and promises made to Israel’s fathers.

chapters.n: He instructs the servant to watch and care for the tree.
The natural branches will be hidden in the “nethermost”—most remote—parts of the vineyard. God scatters Israel to preserve it, not just punish it.

f.g: Farthest, lowest parts.
Store harvest—symbolizing souls saved for God.

chapters.n: The Lord hides the natural branches in various remote places, as he wishes. Lehi’s family is one such branch, led to the Americas.
A long time passes. The master and servant return to work in the vineyard—often understood as the era of Christ’s mortal ministry.
Together they go down to labor; the servant points to the original tree.

f.g: Often understood as the Lord’s prophets and authorized messengers.

chapters.n: The wild branches grafted in are bearing good fruit, like the natural fruit. Gentiles who accepted the gospel became faithful disciples.
The wild branches draw strength from the tree’s roots, so they bear tame fruit. Gentile converts flourished because of Israel’s covenants. Without the graft, the tree would have died.
The master now goes to see if the natural branches hidden far away have borne fruit.
The first hidden branch has produced much good fruit after long nourishing.
The servant is puzzled: why plant there? It was the poorest spot in the vineyard.
“Counsel me not,” the master replies. He knew the ground was poor, yet his care made it fruitful. God can make anything grow.
Another branch was planted in even poorer soil, and it too has borne good fruit.
A third branch also bears fruit under the Lord’s care.
The last branch was planted in a good spot, but only part produced good fruit; the rest is wild. Many see this as the Nephites and Lamanites in the promised land.
The master orders the fruitless branches cut off and burned.
The servant pleads for more time to prune and nourish, hoping for better fruit—a picture of intercession and patience.
Master and servant nourish all the fruit of the vineyard.
Much later, the master says the end is approaching, so he must gather fruit. They return to labor again—a period many link to the time after the early Christian era.

f.g: The last part of earth’s history before Christ’s coming.

chapters.n: Returning to the original tree, they find it loaded with all sorts of fruit.
The master tastes every kind of fruit, noting he has gathered much good fruit over time.
Now, though, none of the fruit is good—all kinds of bad fruit. Many understand this as the Great Apostasy, when Christ’s Church lost its authority and purity.

f.w: none of it which is good

chapters.n: The master asks what can be done to save good fruit from the tree.
The servant points out the roots are still alive because the wild branches nourished them.
Yet roots and tree are useless while the fruit is evil.
Still, the master knows the roots are good and has preserved them for his purposes. God’s covenant promises remain even when people fail.
The wild branches overran the roots, producing evil fruit. Without action, the tree will soon be ripe for burning.

f.g: Fully ready—here, ready for judgment.

chapters.n: They go to check whether the hidden natural branches have also gone bad.
All the natural branches—first, second, and last—have become corrupt too. Apostasy is widespread.
In the last branch, the wild part overcame the good part completely; the good branch withered and died. This matches the Nephites’ destruction by the Lamanites.

f.w: the branch had withered away and died

chapters.n: One of scripture’s most moving lines: the master weeps and asks, “What could I have done more for my vineyard?” God grieves for his children.

f.w: the Lord of the vineyard wept

chapters.n: Everything has gone bad; now every tree seems fit only to be cut down and burned.

f.g: Chopped down.

chapters.n: The last tree was planted in the choicest spot—the promised land.

f.w: choice unto me above all other

chapters.n: The master cleared away what occupied that land to plant this tree—perhaps the Jaredites, destroyed before Lehi arrived.

f.w: cut down that which cumbered this spot

chapters.n: Because the bad branches were not removed, they overcame the good branch.
Despite all their care, every tree has become like the wild olive. The master is grieved to lose them.
What more could the master have done? He has worked “almost all the day long,” and asks: who corrupted my vineyard?

f.g: Fertilized with manure.

chapters.n: The servant answers: “loftiness”—pride. The branches grew faster than the roots could support, taking strength to themselves. Pride and self-reliance cut people off from their spiritual roots.

f.g: Height; pride and arrogance.

chapters.n: The master proposes cutting down and burning everything; he has done all he could.
Again the servant pleads, “Spare it a little longer.”
The Lord agrees, because he hates to lose his trees. Mercy delays judgment.
The plan for the final work: take the scattered natural branches and graft them back into the original tree, replacing the most bitter branches. This represents the latter-day gathering of Israel.

f.w: graft them into the tree from whence they came

chapters.n: This is done to keep the tree alive and preserve its roots for God’s purposes.
The scattered branches’ roots are still alive, so branches from the mother tree will be grafted into them too. Gathering flows in both directions.

f.g: The original olive tree—Israel at its source.

chapters.n: They graft from the original tree into the scattered natural trees.
And from the scattered trees back into the mother tree.
Only the most bitter wild branches are removed at first, replaced with the right grafts.
They nourish and trim the trees and remove ripened, doomed branches.
The goal is for the roots to gain strength and the good to overcome the evil.
By preserving the natural branches and roots, the master hopes for good fruit again and joy in his vineyard.

f.w: have joy again in the fruit of my vineyard

chapters.n: He calls more servants to labor with all their might, to bring back the natural fruit—most precious of all.
This is the last time he will prune his vineyard. Latter-day Saints see this as the last dispensation, beginning with the Restoration.
Start with the last, so the last become first and the first last—echoing Jesus’ teaching about the order of the gospel’s spread.

f.w: the last that they may be first

chapters.n: Dig, prune, and fertilize once more. If the new grafts take, clear the way for them to grow.
Remove bad branches gradually as the good grows. Removing them all at once could kill the graft. God’s work proceeds patiently.

f.w: not clear away the bad thereof all at once

chapters.n: Keep root and top balanced in strength until the good overcomes the bad, then the bad will be removed and burned.

f.w: the root and the top may be equal
f.g: Balanced growth—covenant foundations matching outward expansion.

chapters.n: The natural branches will be grafted back into the natural tree.
Natural branches and tree will be reunited, bear natural fruit, and “be one”—a unified covenant people.
The bad will be cast out of the entire vineyard. This pruning happens only once.
The servant brings other servants—but they are few. The final work is done by a small number of laborers.
Labor with your might—this is the last nourishing, and the season is near. Those who work with the Lord will share his joy.
The servants work hard, and the Lord works alongside them. They obey in everything.

f.w: the Lord of the vineyard labored also with them

chapters.n: Natural fruit returns; natural branches flourish; wild branches are removed gradually, root and top kept in balance.
Eventually the bad is gone, the trees bear natural fruit again, and they become “like unto one body.”
The Lord blesses his diligent servants: because they labored with him and brought back the natural fruit, they will share his joy.
He will store up fruit for a long time—widely understood as the Millennium, a long era of peace and righteousness.
When evil returns at the end, good and bad will be separated, and the vineyard—the earth—will be burned and renewed. The allegory spans all of history to the end of the world.

f.w: good and the bad to be gathered

chapters.n: Jacob gives his promised prophecy: everything Zenos said about Israel as an olive tree will surely happen.
When the Lord reaches out “the second time” to gather Israel, it will be the final season of his servants nourishing and pruning the vineyard. Then the end will come.
Those who labor faithfully in the vineyard are blessed; those cast out are cursed. The world will end in fire.

God is merciful: he remembers all Israel, roots and branches, and keeps his hands stretched out all day long, even to a stubborn, argumentative people. Anyone who doesn’t harden their heart will be saved.

f.g: Contradicting, talking back.

f.w: stretches forth his hands unto them all the day long

chapters.n: Jacob pleads: repent wholeheartedly and cling to God as he clings to you. While his merciful arm is extended, don’t harden your hearts.

f.w: cleave unto God as he cleaveth unto you
f.g: Cleave = hold fast, stick closely.

chapters.n: “Today, if ye will hear his voice”—Jacob quotes the Psalms and Ezekiel. Why choose spiritual death?

f.w: today, if ye will hear his voice

chapters.n: After being nourished by God’s word all day long, will you still bear evil fruit and be cut down? Jacob ties the allegory directly to his listeners.
Will you reject the prophets, the testimonies of Christ, the Holy Ghost, and mock the plan of redemption made for you?
Christ’s power of resurrection will bring everyone before God. Those who rejected him will stand there ashamed and guilty.

f.w: stand with shame and awful guilt

chapters.n: Justice cannot be denied. The unrepentant face the “lake of fire and brimstone,” a symbol of endless anguish.
So repent, enter the narrow gate, and stay on the narrow path until you gain eternal life.
A short, heartfelt plea: be wise. He has said all he can.
Jacob says farewell until he meets his hearers at God’s judgment—pleasing to the righteous, terrifying to the wicked.
Years later a man named Sherem arrives among the Nephites. He is the first of several “anti-Christs” in the Book of Mormon.

f.g: First of three notable anti-Christ figures, with Nehor (Alma 1) and Korihor (Alma 30).

chapters.n: Sherem preached that there would be no Christ and flattered the people to undermine the doctrine of Christ.
He drew many away, and since Jacob believed in Christ, Sherem sought chances to confront him.
Sherem was well educated and a skillful speaker, using flattery and eloquence empowered by the devil.

f.g: Mastery of speech and rhetoric.

chapters.n: Sherem hoped to shake Jacob’s faith, but Jacob had seen angels and heard the Lord’s voice many times. Personal revelation made him unshakable.
Sherem approaches politely—“Brother Jacob”—saying he’s heard Jacob preaching what he calls the gospel.

f.g: In this way.

chapters.n: Sherem accuses Jacob of leading people away from the law of Moses and turning it into worship of a future being. He calls it blasphemy, claiming no one can know the future.

f.g: Speaking irreverently about God or sacred things.

f.w: he cannot tell of things to come

chapters.n: The Lord filled Jacob with the Spirit, and he answered every argument.

f.g: Confuse, refute, leave without answer.

chapters.n: Jacob asks directly: do you deny Christ? Sherem says he wouldn’t if Christ existed—but he “knows” there is no Christ.
Jacob asks if Sherem believes the scriptures. Sherem says yes.
Then he doesn’t understand them, Jacob replies—every prophet has testified of Christ.

f.w: none of the prophets have written

chapters.n: Jacob adds his personal witness by the Holy Ghost: without Christ’s Atonement, all humanity would be lost.
Sherem demands a sign by the Holy Ghost.
Jacob refuses to “tempt God” for a sign of what Sherem already knows is true. But he submits it to God: if God strikes Sherem, let that be the sign. Jacob echoes Christ: “Thy will… be done.”

f.w: thy will, O Lord, be done

f.g: Test or challenge God.

chapters.n: The Lord’s power came upon Sherem and he collapsed. He had to be cared for many days.

f.g: Cared for, nursed.

chapters.n: Sensing he will die, Sherem asks the people to gather so he can speak to them.
Before the crowd, Sherem retracts his teachings and confesses Christ, the Holy Ghost, and the ministering of angels.
He admits the devil deceived him and warns of hell and eternal punishment.

f.w: deceived by the power of the devil

chapters.n: Sherem fears he committed the unpardonable sin by lying to God—denying Christ while claiming to believe the scriptures that testify of him.
With those words, he dies.

f.g: Died; breathed his last.

chapters.n: Seeing his deathbed confession, the people were so astonished that God’s power overcame them and they fell to the earth.
Jacob is grateful—he had prayed for this outcome, and God answered.
Peace and God’s love returned. The people studied the scriptures and ignored Sherem’s teachings.
The Nephites tried many ways to bring the Lamanites back to truth, but failed; the Lamanites loved war and harbored lasting hatred.

f.g: Deep-rooted, long-lasting hostility, passed down through generations.

chapters.n: The Nephites fortified themselves and trusted God, their “rock,” and so continued to prevail.

Old now, Jacob reflects that life passed like a dream. His people felt lonely and solemn—wanderers cast out from Jerusalem, born in hardship and hated by their brothers. A poignant, honest reflection.

f.g: Isolated and serious-minded, far from their homeland.

f.w: born in tribulation, in a wilderness

chapters.n: Near death, Jacob gives the plates to his son Enos, who promises to obey Nephi’s instructions. Jacob says farewell with the French-derived “adieu”—“to God.”

f.g: Farewell; from French “à Dieu,” “to God.” Joseph Smith’s translation used this word.
